title: Rejected at Home, a Prophet Beheaded, Bread in the Wilderness
summary: Jesus is rejected in his hometown of Nazareth, then sends the Twelve out two by two to preach repentance and heal. Mark pauses to tell how Herod Antipas had John the Baptist beheaded at a banquet. When the apostles return, Jesus feeds five thousand men from five loaves and two fish, walks on the sea to his struggling disciples, and heals crowds at Gennesaret.
story:
Chapters 4 and 5 showed Jesus' authority over the sea, demons, disease, and death, and ended with a dead girl raised to life. Chapter 6 turns to how people respond to that authority. His own town takes offense, a ruler mistakes him for John come back from the dead, and even his disciples, who have just been sharing his work, fail to understand what they have seen. The chapter opens the section of Mark scholars often call the bread section (6:30 to 8:26), where loaves, meals, sea crossings, and blindness recur until Peter's confession in chapter 8; the word bread (artos) appears seven times in this chapter alone.

The chapter also widens Jesus' work. For the first time he sends the Twelve out with his own authority, fulfilling the purpose for which he appointed them in 3:14, and their mission spreads his name so far that it reaches the ruler of Galilee. It casts a shadow forward as well. John's arrest had marked the start of Jesus' preaching (1:14); now Mark tells how John died, at the hands of a ruler who respected him but would not lose face before his guests, a preview of what will happen to Jesus under Pilate. Between the story of a prophet's death and a meal in the wilderness, Mark sets two banquets side by side, Herod's feast of power and Jesus' feast of compassion.
historical:
Nazareth was a small farming village in the hills of lower Galilee, perhaps a few hundred people. It is not mentioned in the Old Testament, in Josephus, or in the Mishnah, and the earliest non-Christian reference to it is a fragmentary Hebrew inscription found at Caesarea in 1962, usually dated to the third or fourth century AD, listing the places where the priestly courses settled after AD 70. The city of Sepphoris, which Herod Antipas rebuilt as his capital after 4 BC (Josephus, Antiquities 18.27), stood about four miles (six kilometers) to the north, and some scholars have suggested that a builder from Nazareth could have found work there, though the Gospels never mention it.

The Herod of this chapter is Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, who ruled Galilee and Perea from 4 BC to AD 39. Rome gave him the title tetrarch, a ruler of part of a kingdom, and Matthew and Luke use it (Matthew 14:1, Luke 9:7); Mark's ‘King Herod’ may reflect popular usage, and it carries an irony his readers may have known, since Antipas later asked the emperor Gaius (Caligula) for the royal title and instead, accused by his nephew Agrippa I, was exiled to Lugdunum in Gaul in AD 39, where Herodias chose to follow him (Antiquities 18.240-256). Josephus also tells of John's death (Antiquities 18.116-119). He calls John a good man who urged the Jews to practice justice toward one another and piety toward God and to come together for baptism, and he says that Antipas, fearing that John's influence over the crowds might lead to revolt, sent him in chains to the fortress of Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea, and put him to death there. Mark gives the personal motive, Josephus the political one, and the two can stand together, since a prophet who publicly condemned the ruler's marriage was also a public threat. Nearly all scholars accept the passage in Josephus as genuine.

The marriage itself was a scandal with international consequences. Josephus says that Antipas, visiting his half-brother in Rome, fell in love with his wife Herodias, who was also the granddaughter of Herod the Great and so Antipas's niece; they agreed that she would leave her husband and that Antipas would divorce his first wife, a daughter of the Nabatean king Aretas IV (Antiquities 18.109-110). The law forbade marrying a brother's wife while the brother lived (Leviticus 18:16, 20:21), and Josephus himself says Herodias acted in defiance of the ancestral laws (Antiquities 18.136). Aretas later defeated Antipas in battle, around AD 36, and Josephus reports that some Jews saw the defeat as God's punishment for the killing of John (18.116). Josephus calls Herodias's first husband Herod and says that her daughter Salome married Philip the tetrarch (18.136-137), while Mark calls the first husband Philip (see the second hard question). Excavations at Machaerus by a Hungarian team under Győző Vörös, from 2009, have uncovered the Herodian palace there, including a peristyle courtyard in which Vörös identified the setting of a royal throne, the kind of hall in which a banquet like Herod's could have been held.

The feeding and the crossing take place around the north end of the lake. Bethsaida, near where the Jordan enters the lake, lay in the territory of Philip the tetrarch, who refounded it as Julias (Antiquities 18.28); its site is disputed between et-Tell, excavated by Rami Arav from 1987, and el-Araj, excavated since 2016 by a team under Mordechai Aviam and R. Steven Notley. Gennesaret was the fertile plain on the northwest shore, which Josephus describes as so rich that walnuts, palms, figs, olives, and grapes all grow there together (Jewish War 3.516-521).
cultural:
The word translated carpenter (tektōn) covers a builder or craftsman in wood or stone. Justin Martyr, writing in Rome around AD 155, says Jesus made ploughs and yokes as a carpenter (Dialogue with Trypho 88). A village craftsman had honor as a working man but no standing as a teacher, and the people of Nazareth cannot reconcile the wisdom and mighty works they hear about with the man whose family they know. Calling a man the son of his mother rather than his father was unusual; it may reflect that Joseph had died, or it may carry a hint of the rumors surrounding his birth. Two of the brothers named here are known elsewhere. James led the Jerusalem church (Galatians 1:19, Acts 15:13), and Josephus records his stoning in AD 62, calling him the brother of Jesus who was called Christ (Antiquities 20.200); Judas is traditionally the author of the Letter of Jude, and Eusebius, citing the second-century writer Hegesippus, tells of his grandsons, farmers questioned under the emperor Domitian (Church History 3.20). Christians have understood these brothers and sisters in three ways: as later children of Joseph and Mary (argued by Helvidius in the fourth century and held by most Protestants), as children of Joseph by an earlier marriage (Epiphanius, the Protevangelium of James, and the Eastern Orthodox tradition), or as cousins (Jerome, Against Helvidius, around 383, and much Western Catholic teaching).

The mission instructions assume Jewish hospitality. The Twelve carry a staff and wear sandals but take no bread, no money, and no bag (pēra), the pouch that was the badge of the wandering Cynic philosophers; Diogenes Laertius says Antisthenes was the first to double his cloak and carry a staff and a wallet (Lives of the Philosophers 6.13), and John Dominic Crossan (The Historical Jesus, 1991) made the comparison central to his portrait of Jesus. The difference is telling: the Cynic begged, but the Twelve are to receive hospitality and stay put. Josephus says the Essenes traveled carrying nothing except weapons against bandits because members of their community in every town took them in (Jewish War 2.124-125), and the Didache, an early Christian manual, later warns that a traveling apostle who stays more than two days or asks for money is a false prophet (Didache 11.4-6). Shaking dust from the feet was a public sign of breaking off (compare Nehemiah 5:13, Acts 13:51); the Babylonian Talmud credits two sages of the second century BC, Yose ben Yoezer and Yose ben Yohanan, with a decree that the soil of Gentile lands conveyed impurity (b. Shabbat 15a), and applied to a Jewish town the gesture treats it as foreign ground. Olive oil was the ordinary medicine of the Mediterranean world (Isaiah 1:6, Luke 10:34), and James 5:14 later tells elders to anoint the sick with it.

Herod's banquet belongs to a world Jewish readers knew from Scripture. Birthday feasts were a royal custom: Pharaoh's birthday feast ended with one servant restored and another hanged (Genesis 40:20-22), and 2 Maccabees 6:7 remembers Jews forced to join the monthly celebration of Antiochus's birthday. Herod's oath before his nobles bound him in an honor culture where public words could not be taken back without shame, and his promise of up to half his kingdom echoes the Persian king's words to Esther (Esther 5:3, 7:2), a promise all the more hollow since Antipas held his territory at Rome's pleasure. Roman historians told similar stories of an execution at a banquet as the mark of a tyrant; Livy tells how the consul Lucius Flamininus had a condemned man put to death at dinner to please a companion and was expelled from the Senate for it (History of Rome 39.42-43). In the wilderness meal, a denarius was a laborer's daily wage (Matthew 20:2), so two hundred denarii was most of a year's income. The head of a Jewish household said a blessing over bread before a meal, blessing God who brings forth bread from the earth (m. Berakhot 6:1), and then broke and shared it. The baskets (kophinoi) were the stiff wicker baskets that the Roman satirist Juvenal twice associates with Jews (Satires 3.14, 6.542). The Romans divided the night into four watches, so the fourth ran from about 3 to 6 in the morning, and belief in night apparitions (phantasmata) was widespread. At Gennesaret the sick ask to touch the kraspedon of his cloak, the tassel the law told Israelite men to wear at the corners of their garments as a reminder of the commandments (Numbers 15:38-39).
literary:
Mark uses one of his sandwiches here: the Twelve are sent out (verses 7 to 13), the story of John's death fills the gap (14 to 29), and the apostles return (30). The frame links mission and martyrdom, so that the reader learns during the first mission that those who preach repentance may meet John's end. The story of John is itself told as a flashback, the only passage in Mark in which Jesus does not appear, and it is shaped by the Old Testament. Herod and Herodias play Ahab and Jezebel to John's Elijah: a weak king who half respects the prophet, a queen who wants him dead (1 Kings 19:2, 21:25), and a prophet whom Mark has dressed like Elijah (1:6, compare 2 Kings 1:8) and whom Jesus will call the Elijah who has come, to whom they did whatever they wished (9:13). The difference is that this Jezebel succeeds. The banquet also borrows the court language of Esther, the half-kingdom promised to a girl who pleases the king.

The feeding and the sea crossing are told with dense Old Testament echoes. The wilderness place recalls Israel fed with manna; the sheep without a shepherd recall Moses' prayer for a successor so that the congregation will not be “like sheep without a shepherd” (Numbers 27:17) and God's promise to set over his scattered flock “one shepherd, My servant David” (Ezekiel 34:23). The green grass where the people lie down may echo the green pastures of Psalm 23:2, and the groups of hundreds and fifties recall Israel's ordering in the wilderness under leaders of thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens (Exodus 18:21), a pattern the Qumran community also used for its assemblies (1QS 2:21-22). Elisha's feeding of a hundred men with twenty loaves ended with the promise “They will eat and have some left over” (2 Kings 4:43), and Jesus' feeding exceeds it. The Greek has a vivid Semitic idiom in verses 39 and 40: the people sat down symposia symposia, ‘party by party’, and prasiai prasiai, ‘garden bed by garden bed’, so that the crowd looks like rows of planted beds on the green grass. The four verbs of verse 41, took, blessed, broke, gave, return at the second feeding (8:6) and the Last Supper (14:22).

The sea crossing is the second of Mark's three boat scenes and deliberately recalls the first (4:35-41). There Jesus was in the boat asleep; here he is absent, praying on the mountain, and comes to them across the water. Mark says he intended to pass by them, a phrase from the Old Testament's great appearances of God, when the Lord's glory passed by Moses (Exodus 33:22, 34:6) and Elijah on the mountain (1 Kings 19:11), and Job says of God, who “treads on the waves of the sea”, “Were He to pass by me, I would not see Him” (Job 9:8, 11). John Paul Heil (Jesus Walking on the Sea, 1981) classified the story as a sea-rescue epiphany. Jesus' words, “Take courage! It is I,” use the Greek egō eimi, ‘I am’, which is both an ordinary self-identification and the phrase the Greek Old Testament uses for God's self-naming (Exodus 3:14, Isaiah 43:10). The scene ends not with worship, as in Matthew 14:33, but with astonishment and hardened hearts, the note on which Mark closes the chapter's teaching about the loaves.

outline.t: The Twelve sent out two by two
The death of John the Baptist
The apostles return and five thousand are fed

doctrines.note: Unbelief in Nazareth limits what Jesus does there, and the disciples' hardened hearts keep them from understanding the loaves. Faith in Mark is not a technique that produces miracles but a trust that receives what Jesus offers; its absence closes the door from the human side, and Jesus is amazed at it (verse 6).

Jesus shares his authority with the Twelve and sends them to preach repentance, travel light, and depend on others' hospitality. They go in pairs, as the law required two witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15), and their message is Jesus' own (1:15). Mark calls them apostles, those sent, when they return from this first mission (verse 30), the one place in the Gospel where the title is secure in all manuscripts.

John's death shows the cost of speaking God's word to power. Mark places it at the center of the disciples' first mission, so that the reader learns early that faithful witness can end in a prison. John is killed not for a crime but for telling a ruler the truth, and his disciples bury him, as Jesus will be buried after a ruler's weak consent to an innocent man's death (15:15, 15:46).

The chapter shows Jesus in the roles of Israel's anointed. He is the prophet without honor at home (verse 4) whom the people compare to Elijah and the prophets (verse 15); he is the shepherd-king who has compassion on a leaderless people and feeds them (verse 34, Ezekiel 34:23); and his taking, blessing, and breaking of bread anticipates the meal at which he will give himself (14:22).

In Nazareth Jesus is a village builder with a mother, brothers, and sisters, amazed at his neighbors' unbelief; on the lake he treads the waves as only God does (Job 9:8) and names himself with the words “It is I.” Mark sets the two scenes in one chapter, and the church confesses both as true of one person.

words.note: Tektōn, craftsman, builder, most often in wood but also in stone and metal. It occurs only twice in the New Testament: here, where Jesus himself is the tektōn, and Matthew 13:55, where he is the tektōn's son. BDAG gives builder or carpenter. The word placed Jesus among ordinary working men, which is exactly why his hometown could not accept his wisdom. Origen told the pagan critic Celsus that Jesus is nowhere called a carpenter in the church's Gospels (Against Celsus 6.36), which suggests that his copy of Mark read ‘son of the carpenter’ (see text).

Skandalizō, to cause to stumble, to take offense, to fall away. It occurs 29 times in the New Testament, eight in Mark; the noun skandalon is a trap or stumbling block. The people of Nazareth trip over Jesus' ordinariness. Mark uses the same verb in the explanation of the sower for those who fall away when trouble comes (4:17) and in 14:27, when Jesus predicts that all the disciples will fall away. Offense at Jesus is not only the outsiders' reaction.

Apostolos, one sent, a messenger or envoy. It occurs about 79 times in the New Testament, mostly in Luke, Acts, and Paul, but securely only once in Mark, here in verse 30; at 3:14 the clause naming the Twelve apostles is present in Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus but absent from many manuscripts, and some editors think it was borrowed from Luke 6:13. The word matches the verb apostellō, to send, in verse 7: they are called apostles when they return from being sent.

Splagchnizomai, to have compassion, from splagchna, the inner organs, where ancient people located deep feeling. It occurs twelve times in the New Testament, only in the first three Gospels, and always of Jesus or of figures in his parables who stand for God's mercy, such as the Samaritan (Luke 10:33) and the prodigal's father (Luke 15:20). Here it moves Jesus to teach and then feed a crowd that had interrupted the rest he planned for his tired apostles (verses 31 and 34).

Kophinos, a stiff wicker basket for carrying food or goods. It occurs six times in the New Testament, always of the twelve baskets left over after the feeding of the five thousand (Matthew 14:20, 16:9; Mark 6:43, 8:19; Luke 9:17; John 6:13). At the second feeding Mark uses spuris, a larger basket (8:8), and Jesus later reminds the disciples of both numbers and both kinds (8:19-20). Twelve baskets, one for each of the Twelve, may also recall Israel's twelve tribes.

Parerchomai, to pass by, go past, pass away. It occurs 29 times in the New Testament. In verse 48 it is the verb of the Greek Old Testament's accounts of God passing by Moses (Exodus 33:19, 22) and Elijah (1 Kings 19:11), and Job 9:11 in the Greek uses it of God passing by unseen. Read against that background, Jesus' intention to pass by the boat is not indifference but the language of divine self-revelation, as Heil and many commentators have argued; others read it simply as Jesus meaning to go ahead of them, and the text allows both.

Pōroō, to harden, to make callous or dull. It occurs five times in the New Testament: twice in Mark of the disciples (6:52, 8:17), and in John 12:40, Romans 11:7, and 2 Corinthians 3:14 of Israel's hardening. The related noun pōrōsis is used of the Pharisees' hardness in 3:5. Mark applies the word not to Jesus' opponents here but to his own disciples, a startling honesty: in Scripture hardness of heart is a settled incapacity to perceive, and insiders are not immune.

Kraspedon, edge, border, and in Jewish use the tassel (Hebrew tsitsit) worn at the corners of a garment by command of the law (Numbers 15:38-39, Deuteronomy 22:12). It occurs five times in the New Testament: of the woman who touched Jesus' tassel (Matthew 9:20, Luke 8:44), of the Pharisees who lengthen theirs (Matthew 23:5), and of the crowds at Gennesaret (Matthew 14:36, Mark 6:56). The sick reach for the sign of the commandments on the garment of an observant Jew and are healed.

christ:
The chapter shows Jesus as prophet, shepherd, and more than either. He accepts the prophet's lot of rejection at home, a pattern as old as Jeremiah, whose own townsmen of Anathoth plotted against him (Jeremiah 11:21), and John's fate foreshadows his own. Herod's fear that John has been raised also anticipates, in distorted form, the church's proclamation of a resurrection: the reader knows that it will be Jesus, not John, who is raised, and that his tomb, unlike John's, will be found empty.

In the wilderness Jesus has compassion on a people who are like sheep without a shepherd. Moses had prayed that the Lord's people would not be left in that state (Numbers 27:17), and through Ezekiel God promised to gather his scattered flock and set over them “one shepherd, My servant David” (Ezekiel 34:23), while Isaiah says of the Lord himself, “He tends His flock like a shepherd” (Isaiah 40:11). Jesus teaches, orders the people as Moses ordered Israel, and feeds them as God fed Israel with manna and as Elisha fed a hundred men, but on a scale that exceeds them all. Some Jews expected the Messiah to preside at a banquet at the end of days; the Rule of the Congregation from Qumran (1QSa 2:11-22) describes a meal at which the priest blesses the bread and the Messiah of Israel then stretches out his hand to it. The words took, blessed, broke, and gave point ahead to the bread Jesus will give as his body (14:22), and Christians from the earliest centuries have read the feeding in the light of the Lord's Supper.

On the sea he does what the Old Testament reserves for God, who alone “treads on the waves of the sea” (Job 9:8), whose way is through the sea though his footprints are unseen (Psalm 77:19), and who passed by Moses and Elijah to reveal himself. He names himself with the words that stand behind God's name. The disciples do not yet understand, which is part of Mark's point: who Jesus is cannot be fully grasped until the cross and resurrection explain the bread, and the first human being in Mark to call him the Son of God will be a Roman centurion at the cross (15:39).
interpretation:
The Nazareth scene raised questions from early on. The pagan critic Celsus mocked Christians for worshiping a carpenter, and Origen replied that Jesus is nowhere called a carpenter in the church's Gospels (Against Celsus 6.36), apparently reading ‘the son of the carpenter’. Justin Martyr (Dialogue with Trypho 88) says Jesus made ploughs and yokes. The brothers and sisters of verse 3 were at the center of a fourth-century controversy: Helvidius argued that they were Mary's later children, and Jerome answered in Against Helvidius (around 383) that they were cousins, while Epiphanius and the Eastern tradition held them to be Joseph's children by an earlier marriage. Verse 5 became a classic text for the question of how Jesus' power relates to human faith, and B. H. Streeter (The Four Gospels, 1924) used Matthew's change from ‘could not’ to ‘did not’ (Matthew 13:58) as a prime example of Matthew smoothing Mark out of reverence, an argument for Mark's priority.

John's death became one of the most painted scenes in Christian art. The church keeps the memorial of his beheading on August 29, when the Roman calendar reads Mark 6:17-29, and shrines in Damascus, now within the Umayyad Mosque, and elsewhere have claimed his head; Muslims also honor him as the prophet Yahya. Donatello's gilt bronze Feast of Herod (completed 1427) for the baptismal font in Siena's baptistery was one of the first works to use the new science of linear perspective, and Caravaggio's Beheading of Saint John the Baptist (1608), in the Co-Cathedral of St. John in Valletta, is the only painting he signed, in the blood flowing from John's neck. The unnamed girl of Mark's story became Salome, a figure of fatal seduction in Oscar Wilde's play Salomé (written in French in 1891, first performed in Paris in 1896), which invented the Dance of the Seven Veils, and in Richard Strauss's opera Salome (Dresden, 1905). Historians have weighed Mark's account against Josephus: Gerd Theissen (The Gospels in Context) argued that it reflects a popular story current in Palestine, Harold Hoehner (Herod Antipas, 1972) defended its general reliability, and Ross Kraemer (Journal of Biblical Literature, 2006) argued that the blame placed on Herodias and her daughter is historically unlikely.

The feeding was read eucharistically from early on. The loaves and fishes appear in the Roman catacombs, and a fifth-century mosaic at Tabgha on the lake's northwest shore, in the Church of the Multiplication, shows a basket of loaves between two fish before the altar. Rationalist critics of the Enlightenment sought natural explanations. H. E. G. Paulus (Das Leben Jesu, 1828) proposed that Jesus' example shamed people into sharing food they had brought and that Jesus was walking by the sea, on the shore, not on it; David Friedrich Strauss (The Life of Jesus, 1835) answered Paulus that such readings distort the texts and read both stories as myths built from Old Testament models. Modern commentators generally read them as the Evangelists meant them, as disclosures of who Jesus is. In the lectionaries the Revised Common Lectionary reads 6:1-13, 6:14-29, and 6:30-34 with 53-56 on successive Sundays in July in Year B (Propers 9 to 11) and then turns to John 6 for the feeding and the bread of life; the Roman Lectionary reads Mark 6 on the fourteenth to sixteenth Sundays in Ordinary Time and likewise turns to John 6 on the seventeenth.
text:
Several differences between English Bibles in this chapter come from manuscripts. In verse 3 nearly all manuscripts read ‘the carpenter, the son of Mary’, but a few, apparently including the early papyrus P45 and some Old Latin copies, read ‘the son of the carpenter and of Mary’, which agrees with Matthew 13:55; scribes may have wished to avoid a lowly title for Jesus. In verse 11 later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, add a sentence borrowed from Matthew 10:15, that it will be more tolerable for Sodom and Gomorrah on the day of judgment than for that city. In verse 14 the earliest witnesses (Codex Vaticanus, Codex Bezae, and some Old Latin) read ‘they were saying’, so the opinion that John was raised belongs to people generally (BSB, ‘people were saying’); most later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read ‘he said’, making it Herod's own view from the start.

In verse 20 the earliest manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and a few others) read polla ēporei, ‘he was greatly perplexed’, while most later ones, followed by the KJV's ‘he did many things’, read polla epoiei. The two words differ by a few letters, and modern editions prefer the first, which fits the picture of a man torn between conscience and pride. In verse 22 Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Vaticanus, and Codex Bezae read ‘his daughter Herodias’, which would make the girl Antipas's own daughter, named for her mother, and the Nestle-Aland Greek text has printed it since 1979; the NRSV follows it. Most later manuscripts read ‘the daughter of Herodias herself’, which the BSB and most versions follow and which agrees with Josephus, who names her Salome, Herodias's daughter by her first husband. Verse 20's ‘protected him’ (suntēreō, ‘kept him safe’) is ‘observed him’ in the KJV, an older sense of the English word.

teach.big: Jesus comes as the rejected prophet, the compassionate shepherd, and the Lord of the sea, and the question the chapter presses is whether those who see him, in his hometown, at court, and in his own boat, will receive him or harden their hearts.

outline.t: Familiarity can blind us: people who think they already know Jesus may be the ones who cannot receive him.
Jesus shares his authority with ordinary disciples and sends them out dependent, together, and with his message of repentance.
A guilty conscience hears the news about Jesus and fears judgment rather than seeking mercy.
Faithful witness can cost everything, and power without courage will sacrifice the righteous to save face.
Jesus' compassion meets the whole need, teaching and bread, and he makes his disciples the servants of his abundance.
Jesus sees his people straining against the wind and comes to them as God comes, but understanding his provision requires a softened heart.
Those who know their need reach for Jesus wherever he goes, and all who touch him are made well.

teach.pitfalls:
Verse 5 is often misused in two opposite directions. Some teach that faith is a force that makes miracles happen and that unbelief is the reason any prayer goes unanswered; Mark says Jesus still healed a few in Nazareth, and his point is personal trust, not a spiritual technique. Others dismiss the verse as embarrassing; it shows Jesus' real humanity and the seriousness of refusing him. The mission instructions of verses 8 and 9 are sometimes turned into a rule that ministers must be poor or that churches must never pay their workers; they are instructions for a specific short mission, and elsewhere Jesus changes them for a new situation (Luke 22:35-36).

The story of John's death should not become a morality tale about dancing or about women as temptresses, which is how later art and literature often used it. The girl is a pawn, Herodias is a person with her own grievance, and the moral weight falls on Herod, who knew John was righteous and killed him anyway. With the feeding, avoid the rationalist reading that the real miracle was everyone sharing their hidden lunches, which Mark's wording does not support, and avoid the opposite error of making it only a lesson in generosity. With the walk on the water, resist turning it into a lesson about stepping out in faith; that comes from Peter's attempt in Matthew's version, while Mark's point is who Jesus is and why the disciples cannot yet see it.
teach.pastoral: The Nazareth scene may press on anyone who has been dismissed by their own family or hometown, including those whose faith is treated with contempt at home; Jesus himself knew that pain. John's death will reach people who have suffered for telling the truth: whistleblowers, those who confronted abuse, those who lost jobs or relationships for refusing to go along. Teach it with honesty that faithfulness is sometimes not rewarded in this life, while pointing to the vindication God gives. Take care with verse 5 around people living with chronic illness or grief: they should not leave thinking that their suffering is proof of weak faith. And the disciples straining at the oars all night, with Jesus watching from the mountain before he comes, may help those who feel God has seen their struggle and left them in it.

hard.q: Mark says Jesus could not perform miracles in Nazareth. Was his power limited by people's unbelief?
hard.a:
The objection comes from the text itself. Mark's wording is blunt (ouk edunato, ‘he was not able’), and Matthew's parallel changes it to “He did not do many miracles there, because of their unbelief” (Matthew 13:58). B. H. Streeter (The Four Gospels, 1924) cited this as a clear case of a later Evangelist softening Mark out of reverence, and critics have drawn the further conclusion that the historical Jesus was a healer whose cures depended on the expectation of those around him, so that where no one expected anything, nothing happened. Mark adds that Jesus was amazed at their unbelief (verse 6), which seems to show surprise and limitation.

Interpreters have answered in several ways. One view is that Jesus' miracles were never displays forced on unwilling people but acts that met faith, so where no one came to him in trust there was little for him to do; the few sick he did heal were presumably those who came. A second view takes could not as a moral rather than a physical impossibility: it would not fit his mission to perform wonders for a town that had already decided against him, just as he refuses to give a sign on demand (8:12). A third notes that in his incarnate life Jesus chose to work in dependence on the Father and the Spirit, and that Mark does not hesitate to show his real humanity, including amazement; how that dependence relates to his divine power has been discussed in different ways in the churches, and Christians hold a range of views on it within the confession of Chalcedon. None of these readings means that human unbelief overpowers God. They mean that Jesus' power is personal, exercised for those who receive him, and that refusing him has real consequences.

hard.q: Can Mark's account of John's death be squared with Josephus?
hard.a:
The critical case points to several tensions. Josephus says John was killed at Machaerus, a desert fortress east of the Dead Sea, for political reasons, because Antipas feared an uprising (Antiquities 18.116-119); Mark tells a court story of a birthday banquet with the leading men of Galilee, a dancing girl, and a vengeful wife. Mark calls Herodias's first husband Philip, while Josephus calls him Herod and says that Philip the tetrarch married Herodias's daughter (18.136-137). Mark calls Antipas king, which Rome never did. Ross Kraemer (Journal of Biblical Literature, 2006) argued that the blame placed on Herodias and her daughter is historically unlikely and serves a Christian theological purpose, and many critical scholars regard the banquet scene as a popular legend modeled on Esther and on the story of Ahab and Jezebel.

Others reply that the two sources agree on the essentials: Antipas imprisoned and executed John, a righteous man with a large following, and the marriage to Herodias was central to the affair, since Josephus himself ties Aretas's war, and the popular verdict that the defeat was God's punishment, to the divorce and to John's death. Motives can be both personal and political. Harold Hoehner (Herod Antipas, 1972) argued that Herodias's first husband may have been known as Herod Philip, since several Herodian princes shared the family name alongside another. Others note that Galilean nobles could have attended their ruler at Machaerus, where excavations have uncovered a palace suited to such a banquet. Gerd Theissen (The Gospels in Context) judged that Mark reflects a story that circulated in Palestine soon after the events, colored by popular feeling against the court, which would explain both its vividness and its imprecisions. Luke mentions people close to Antipas's household who followed Jesus, such as Joanna, the wife of Herod's steward Chuza (Luke 8:3), a possible channel for such stories. Readers who hold a high view of Scripture differ on how to resolve the name of the first husband, and the question does not touch the story's point: a prophet died for telling a ruler the truth.

observe: What questions do the people of Nazareth ask about Jesus, and what does Mark say Jesus could and could not do there?
What are the Twelve told to take and not to take, and what do they do on their mission?
What does Mark say about why the disciples were astounded when Jesus got into the boat (verse 52)?
interpret: Why do you think Mark places the story of John's death in the middle of the account of the Twelve's first mission?
What Old Testament stories and hopes does the feeding in the wilderness bring to mind, and what do they suggest about who Jesus is?
What does it mean that Jesus intended to pass by the disciples and then said, “Take courage! It is I”?
apply: The people of Nazareth could not accept wisdom from someone they thought they already knew. Where might familiarity keep you from hearing God speak?
Herod listened gladly to John and still killed him to save face before his guests. What pressures make it hard for you to act on what you know is right?
Jesus told his tired disciples, “You give them something to eat.” What need in front of you seems too large, and what do you already have that you could place in his hands?
